header.title: De Natura Animalium: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Aelian
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg0545.tlg001.perseus-grc2, from the Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0545.tlg001.perseus-: Several identifications are doubtful: ῥάμνος ‘buckthorn’ (some thorny shrub); κίρκοι ‘hawks’ (perhaps harriers or falcons); *pikris* perhaps a chicory or ox-tongue; *aristereōn* perhaps vervain; *harpē* an unidentified bird of prey; ἄγρωστις ‘couch-grass’. The heron's ‘crab’ (καρκίνος) is odd among plants and may be a plant name.
Seuechorus is unidentified. Gilgamos is generally taken to be Gilgamesh. ‘Having tried as hard as I can to find against it’ (πειρώμενος ἐς ἰσχὺν κατεγνωκέναι αὐτόν) is of uncertain sense.
*Galeōtēs* is probably a gecko, not certainly. ‘Love-charms’ renders ἴυγγας (literally ‘iynxes’, wryneck charms). ‘Old skin’ renders γῆρας, literally ‘old age’, the shed slough.

nodes.text: Even the irrational animals, by some secret and wonderful nature, guard against the eyes of those who cast the evil eye and of sorcerers. I hear, for instance, that as a defence against the evil eye wood pigeons bite off slender sprigs of bay and then place them in their nests, to protect their chicks; kites [use] buckthorn, hawks *pikris* [a bitter herb], turtle-doves the seed of the iris, ravens chaste-tree, hoopoes maidenhair, which some also call *kallitrichon* [‘fair-hair’], the crow *aristereōn* [a herb], the *harpē* [a bird of prey] ivy, the heron a crab, the partridge the plume of a reed, thrushes a sprig of myrtle. The crested lark also puts couch-grass before [its nest], and eagles the stone which is accordingly named *aetitēs* [‘eagle-stone’] after them. This stone is said to be good for pregnant women too, being an enemy of miscarriage.

Euripides calls envy ‘ill-named’; and it seems that it dwells in some animals too. The *galeōtēs* [gecko], for instance, as Theophrastus says, when it has shed its old skin, turns round and swallows it, making it vanish; for the old skin of this creature is thought to be a counter to epilepsy. The stag too knows that its right horn is good for many purposes, and so it buries and hides it, begrudging that anyone should enjoy such great benefits. The mare knows that she brings forth love-charms together with the foal; that is why, as soon as the young one is born, she bites off the bit of flesh on its forehead. People call it *hippomanes*. And the sorcerers say that such things provide and kindle certain impulses that draw towards irrepressible intercourse, and a sexual frenzy. So the mare does not want human beings to share in this charm, as if begrudging them a very great good. Is it not so?

I learn that the Egyptians bring birds down from the sky by a kind of native magic; and having bewitched snakes with certain incantations, they then draw them out of their holes with the greatest ease.

Love of human beings is also characteristic of animals. An eagle, for instance, reared a baby. And I want to tell the whole story, so that it may bear witness to what I have proposed. When Seuechorus was king of the Babylonians, the Chaldeans said that the child born of his daughter would take the kingdom away from his grandfather. He shuddered at this and, if I may say it a little playfully, became an Acrisius towards his daughter, for he guarded her most harshly. But the girl (for fate was cleverer than the Babylonian) secretly gave birth, having been made pregnant by some obscure man. So the guards, for fear of the king, threw [the baby] from the citadel, for that was where the girl was shut up. Then an eagle, very keenly seeing the child while it was still falling, before the baby could be dashed against the ground, flew in beneath it and put its back under it, and carried it to a garden and set it down very gently. The keeper of the place, seeing the beautiful little child, loved it and reared it; and he was called Gilgamos, and became king of the Babylonians. If this seems a fable to anyone, I agree, having tried as hard as I can to find against it; but I do hear that Achaemenes the Persian, from whom the nobility of the Persians descends, was an eagle’s nursling.
